Field observations of the Olive-headed lorikeet (Trichoglossus euteles) in the dry forests of Timor reveal that newly hatched chicks, which emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], remain entirely dependent on parental provisioning for the first weeks of life. The incubation period itself lasts approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days], a duration comparable to that of the closely related coconut lorikeet, Trichoglossus haematodus, from which this estimate is par at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]tially derived. At hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is only about 5.5 grams [Wwb = about 5.5 grams], a remarkably modest mass given that adults of this species are substantial in size. This initial mass represents just a small fraction of the ultimate body weight the chick must achieve before it can achieve flight and independence. The rapid growth trajectory that follows these first few days is sustained by intensive biparental care, with both adults making frequent foraging trips to provision the developing nestling.

Under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of this species active metabolic period, which typically hover around 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones occurs. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and the ability to leave the nest cavity, takes place at approximately 55 days after birth [tx = approximately 55 days after birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively extended nestling period is typical of many small to medium-sized parrots and reflects the time required for the pin-feathered chick to develop fully functional flight feathers and the musculature necessary for aerial locomotion. Following nest departure, the fledgling continues to receive supplementary feedings from its parents for a number of weeks, gradually transitioning to a diet of nectar, pollen, and soft fruits as it hones its foraging skills. This nutritional independence does not occur abruptly but rather over a period of sustained dependence.

Longitudinal data from a captive colony maintained at the University of Indonesia indicate that puberty in Trichoglossus euteles is attained at 165 days after birth [tp = 165 days after birth], when both sexes show the first signs of gonadal activity under those same warm thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This developmental benchmark is somewhat earlier than that reported for the larger Trichoglossus haematodus, which often delays maturation until well past six months of age. The relatively early onset of sexual maturation in the Olive-headed lorikeet may be an adaptation to a seasonally fluctuating resource base, allowing young birds to begin breeding before the onset of a prolonged dry period. Despite achieving puberty at this age, individuals typically do not breed immediately; they often spend several additional months developing adult plumage and acquiring the social status necessary to secure a nesting territory.

The first successful breeding event, or age at first brood, has been recorded at 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth] for individuals maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a value consistent with observations of Trichoglossus haematodus in captivity. This two-year lag between reaching sexual maturity and initiating reproduction is not unusual among lorikeets; it likely reflects the substantial energetic and experiential requirements for successful nesting, including the establishment of a pair bond, the selection and defense of a suitable tree hollow, and the acquisition of sufficient foraging proficiency to support egg production and chick rearing. Clutch size is typically modest, with females laying approximately 3 eggs per breeding attempt [N_R_i = approximately 3 eggs per breeding attempt]. Pairs usually attempt only a single brood during each breeding season [F_R_i = single brood during each breeding season], yielding a relatively low annual reproductive output compared to many passerines of similar body mass.

Adult body mass in the Olive-headed lorikeet reaches an ultimate wet weight of 73.7 grams [Wwi = 73.7 grams], a figure that places it among the mid-sized members of the genus. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually over the first year of life, with most individuals reaching adult proportions by approximately 300 days post-hatching. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, based on banding returns and captive records, stands at 16 years [am = 16 years] under the thermal conditions typical of its active period at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This remarkable longevity for a 74-gram bird underscores the slow life-history pace characteristic of parrots, in which increased survival is traded off against low fecundity.
